Letter to our shareholders




Letter to our shareholders
                                                                                                       Our success is reflected not only in our strong financial results. Our share price perfor-
                                                                                                       mance is a further indicator. MTU’s share price rose again in 2025. In October, our share
                                                                                                       price reached €398.70 – its highest level since MTU’s IPO twenty years ago.

                                                                                                       We want you, our shareholders, to participate appropriately in MTU’s success. At the
                                                                                                       Annual General Meeting in May, we will propose a dividend of €3.60 per share. This cor-
                                                                                                       responds to an increase of €1.40 compared with the previous year.

                                                                                                       In this way, we would like to thank you for your confidence and trust in MTU and in our
                                                                                                       long-term growth prospects. We would also like to thank all our customers and business
                                                                                                       partners worldwide for their long-standing, trusting cooperation, as well as the Super-
                                                                                                       visory Board for its support of our strategic course. Let’s continue writing MTU’s success
                                                                                                       story together!

                                                                                                       You can be assured of one thing: we will not be resting on our laurels. Instead, we are
                                                                                                       focusing on profitable growth, operational excellence, innovation and sustainability – and
                                                                                                       thereby on enhancing the value of our company. Efficiency and cost discipline are of
                                                                                                       crucial importance in this context.

                                                                                                       We will capitalize on our sector’s strong long-term growth prospects. In the next twenty
                                                                                                       years, the number of aircraft in the sky will approximately double. This signifies sus-
                                                                                                       tained demand for new aircraft and a growing need for maintenance solutions. MTU
                                                                                                       is exceptionally positioned to fully benefit from the global growth of aviation – in all
                                                                                                       business areas.

                                                                                                       Consistently high demand in new commercial business was reflected in our trade fair
                                                                                                       successes in 2025. At the Paris Air Show in June, engine orders were placed from which

Letter to our shareholders




Together with Airbus, we want to advance the development of hydrogen fuel cell drives,
a promising and crucial technology for the decarbonization of aviation. This partner-
ship follows Airbus’s decision to focus its own research efforts on an all-electric, hydro-
gen-powered aircraft with fuel cell propulsion. MTU has built up recognized expertise in
this area with its Flying Fuel Cell™ concept and reached important milestones in 2025.
The design of the flying fuel cell was finalized, stack production for the demonstrator
began and the electric motor from our subsidiary eMoSys was successfully tested for the
first time. In addition, we commissioned our first fuel cell test station in Munich.

In 2025, we impressively demonstrated MTU’s operational and innovative strengths. At
the same time, we continued to invest in our future – thereby creating the conditions for
sustainable, competitive and profitable growth.

Behind this success stand our outstanding employees around the world. Without their
expertise, their excellent work and their passion, this performance would not have been
possible. On behalf of the entire Executive Board team, I would like to thank all of them
for their commitment to the benefit of our MTU. Together, we will continue to inspire our
customers, partners and all stakeholders in the years ahead.

We are all looking forward to shaping the future of aviation and raising the bar once
again for 2026. We intend to grow in all business areas – in the commercial engine busi-
ness as well as in the defense and commercial maintenance sectors. Through targeted
investments, we will continue to strengthen and expand our core business, thereby
securing our sustainable growth. In doing so, we will reliably continue on our successful
trajectory with undiminished momentum.

I very much look forward to your continued support on this journey.

Report of the Supervisory Board




                                                                                                       Report of the Supervisory Board

                                                                                                       MTU can look back on another successful fiscal year. The Group is ideally positioned in
                                                                                                       the market, and operationally it is a high performer. This is reflected in the company’s
                                                                                                       sustained profitable growth. Revenue and earnings figures for 2025 are better than
                                                                                                       originally forecast. Adjusted operating profit in particular saw marked growth, along with
                                                                                                       free cash flow. Thanks to its technological edge, balanced portfolio and broad customer
                                                                                                       base, MTU is perfectly positioned to achieve a further rise in revenue and earnings on an
                                                                                                       adjusted basis in 2026, and to go on growing in the years ahead. The following sections
                                                                                                       contain the Supervisory Board’s report on its activities in fiscal year 2025. The Superviso-
                                                                                                       ry Board will continue its close and trustful collaboration with all stakeholders in 2026.

                                                                                                       Monitoring and advisory activities of the Supervisory Board
                                                                                                       In this report, the Supervisory Board provides information in accordance with Section
                                                                                                       171 (2) of the German Stock Corporation Act (AktG) on its activities in fiscal year 2025
                                                                                                       and the results of its review of the annual financial statements and consolidated financial
Gordon Riske
                                                                                                       statements, including the combined management report. In 2025, the Supervisory Board
Chairman of the Supervisory Board
                                                                                                       carried out, fully and with due care, the duties of oversight and advice entrusted to it by
                                                                                                       law, the articles of association, and its rules of procedure.

                                                                                                       It advised the Executive Board on the running of the company on an ongoing basis,
                                                                                                       continually supported and monitored the management of the business activities and
                                                                                                       assured itself that the Executive Board’s dealings were proper and lawful. The Superviso-
                                                                                                       ry Board and its committees were informed and consulted in a direct and timely manner
                                                                                                       on all decisions of consequence for the company. The Executive Board provided the
                                                                                                       members of the Supervisory Board with regular, prompt and comprehensive information
                                                                                                       on the company’s situation. The Supervisory Board received written monthly reports on
                                                                                                       the company’s net assets, financial position and results of operations. At its meetings,
                                                                                                       the Supervisory Board also discussed the business performance of all of MTU’s affiliated
                                                                                                       companies.

                                                                                                       The Executive Board discussed the strategy and all important projects with the Supervi-
                                                                                                       sory Board. After examination and careful deliberation, the Supervisory Board endorsed
                                                                                                       the company’s strategic orientation with its focus on sustainable and profitable organic

Report of the Supervisory Board




Dr. Peter Weckesser and Dr. Detlef Kayser are new members of the Supervisory Board.
Both candidates were elected to the Supervisory Board of MTU at the company’s Annual
General Meeting on May 8, 2025 with almost 99% of the votes.

On December 17, 2024, the Supervisory Board appointed Dr. Johannes Bussmann as the
new CEO; he joined the company’s Executive Board on July 15, 2025 and became CEO of
MTU Aero Engines AG on September 1, 2025.

Katja Garcia Vila has been a member of MTU’s Executive Board since April 2025. On July 1,
2025, she assumed board responsibility for Finance and Information Technology.

Dr. Ottmar Pfänder joined MTU’s Executive Board on January 1, 2026. As Chief Program
Officer he oversees marketing and sales and program management in MTU’s commercial
and military programs as well as MTU Maintenance sites.

Lars Wagner stepped down from the Executive Board on August 31, 2025, Peter Kamer-
itsch on June 30, 2025, and Michael Schreyögg on December 31, 2025. The Supervisory
Board thanks the former members of the Executive Board for their dedicated and suc-
cessful work over the past years and for the smooth handover of their positions.

The Supervisory Board would like to thank the Executive Board for its close and construc-
tive collaboration. It would also like to thank all employees and the Works Council for
their successful work and enormous commitment in 2025. Moreover, the Supervisory
Board is grateful to all MTU’s shareholders for the trust they place in the company.




Munich, March 17, 2026




Gordon Riske
Chairman of the Supervisory Board

The MTU share




                                                                                                   New records on the stock markets
The MTU share                                                                                      In 2025, global equity markets reached new highs. This performance mainly reflected
                                                                                                   declining key interest rates and an overall accommodative monetary policy stance, which
                                                                                                   supported market conditions. To these factors were added robust corporate earnings,
                                                                                                   particularly in the technology sector. The tangible easing of inflation dampened reces-
                                                                                                   sion concerns and also contributed to the positive sentiment. In addition, the partial
                                                                                                   easing of geopolitical tensions boosted investor confidence. At the same time, low bond
                                                                                                   market yields led to increased capital reallocation into equities. Overall, equity markets
                                                                                                   worldwide recorded significant price gains over the course of the year as a whole.

                                                                                                   Germany’s DAX equity index posted significant double-digit growth in 2025. The bench-
                                                                                                   mark index started the year at 20,025 points and surpassed the 23,000-point level in
                                                                                                   the months that followed, before a sharp correction set in during April. Triggered by
                                                                                                   the announcement of new U.S. tariffs and concerns about an escalation of global trade
                                                                                                   conflicts, the DAX fell to its low for the year of 19,671 points. In the weeks that followed, a
                                                                                                   strong recovery began: as early as May, the index climbed above 24,000 points. Over the
                                                                                                   rest of the year, the DAX traded sideways in a range between 23,000 and 24,500 points.
                                                                                                   On October 9, it reached a new all-time high of 24,611 points. The DAX closed the year at
                                                                                                   24,490 points – reflecting a gain of 23.0% compared to the previous year.

                                                                                                   International equity markets also performed well. The U.S. benchmark index, the Dow
                                                                                                   Jones Industrial Average, rose by 13.0%, while the technology-focused Nasdaq 100 re-
                                                                                                   corded an even stronger increase of 20.2%.

                                                                                                   The aviation industry continued on its growth trajectory in 2025. Global passenger
                                                                                                   traffic once again increased significantly, accompanied by growth in air cargo volumes,
                                                                                                   according to the International Air Transport Association (IATA). This positive trend was
                                                                                                   also reflected in the performance of the sector index. The STOXX Europe TMI Aerospace
                                                                                                   & Defense Index, which includes companies such as Airbus, Safran, Rolls-Royce and MTU,
                                                                                                   recorded an exceptionally strong increase in the reporting year and closed with a gain of
                                                                                                   56.5%. In addition to civil aviation, defense sector shares in particular made a significant
                                                                                                   contribution to this performance. These benefited from persistently high defense spend-
                                                                                                   ing and ongoing geopolitical tensions and achieved above-average share price gains.

Intensive investor relations work
MTU again conducted numerous investor relations activities in fiscal year 2025. One-
on-one meetings and investor conferences were held both in person and virtually. One
particular highlight was the MTU Capital Markets Day on June 17, 2025, held as part
of the Paris Air Show. Around 150 investors and analysts attended either in person or
virtually. In addition, the management and the investor relations team used the trade
show as an opportunity for in-depth discussions with 19 investor groups and around
190 participants.

Overall, MTU attended 17 international investor conferences during the reporting year,
including the German Investment Seminar hosted by Commerzbank/Oddo BHF in New
York, the 24th German Corporate Conference by Kepler Cheuvreux in Frankfurt, the 17th
Goldman Sachs Industrials & Autos Week in London and the Bernstein Pan-European
Strategic Decision Premium Review Conference in Paris. In addition, MTU attended other
conferences organized by various banks. In total, MTU recorded over 1,300 investor
contacts in 2025.

Management compensation report




Management compensation report
                                                                                                     The compensation report describes the principles applied in determining the compensa-
                                                                                                     tion for the Executive Board and Supervisory Board of MTU Aero Engines AG, and states
                                                                                                     the amount and composition of that compensation. The management compensation
                                                                                                     report complies with the provisions of Section 162 of the German Stock Corporation Act
                                                                                                     (AktG) and was prepared jointly by the Supervisory Board and the Executive Board.

                                                                                                     Principles of the compensation system for members of the
                                                                                                     Executive Board
                                                                                                     “At the proposal of the Personnel Committee of MTU Aero Engines AG, the Supervisory
                                                                                                     Board decides on a system of compensation for the members of the Executive Board,
                                                                                                     including the material contractual elements such as the total amount of the compensa-
                                                                                                     tion and its breakdown into non-performance-related and performance-related compo-
                                                                                                     nents. The Personnel Committee reviews the appropriateness and market alignment of
                                                                                                     the Executive Board compensation on a regular basis. For this, it also uses the expertise
                                                                                                     of independent external compensation experts with regard to both the compensation
                                                                                                     system and the structure of the target direct compensation compared with relevant stock
                                                                                                     market segments. In the case of MTU, cross-comparisons are made by reference to the
                                                                                                     DAX stock market segment (peer group for cross-group or horizontal comparison). In
                                                                                                     accordance with the statutory requirements, the compensation system is resubmitted to
                                                                                                     the Annual General Meeting for approval no later than every four years or, in deviation
                                                                                                     from this, in the event that the Supervisory Board identifies a need for modifications.
                                                                                                     (ESRS 2 GOV-3-29e)”1

                                                                                                     The current compensation system was designed in accordance with the requirements
                                                                                                     of the act to implement the Second Shareholders’ Rights Directive (ARUG II) and the
                                                                                                     German Corporate Governance Code (GCGC) and was approved by 56.51% at the Annual
                                                                                                     General Meeting on May 8, 2024 (agenda item 8). It has been applied on this basis since
                                                                                                     fiscal year 2024. From the Supervisory Board’s perspective, the relatively low approval of
                                                                                                     the remuneration system was due, in particular, to the authorization of the Supervisory
                                                                                                     Board to grant an additional, performance-related compensation component in special
                                                                                                     exceptional circumstances. Other points identified included the adjustment of the max-
                                                                                                     imum remuneration and individual aspects of the measurement of target achievement
                                                                                                     for performance-related remuneration components. In the run-up to the 2024 Annual
                                                                                                     General Meeting, the Supervisory Board addressed the criticisms of the compensation
                                                                                                     system and published its considerations in this regard: https://www.mtu.de/fileadmin/
                                                                                                     EN/5_Investor_Relations/9_1_Annual_General_Meeting/2024_AGM_A_04_Top_8__further_info_re-
                                                                                                     muneration_system_MTU.pdf.

Malus and clawback clauses
Further, the compensation system for the Executive Board contains malus and claw-back
rules. This enables the Supervisory Board, at its discretion, to reduce performance-relat-
ed components that have not been paid out (malus clause) or claim reimbursement of
performance-related components that have already been paid (clawback clause). The

Members of the Executive Board did not receive any compensation for supervisory board
and similar appointments at Group companies. The Group did not grant any loans to
members of the Executive Board in the reporting period or the previous year.

The compensation of the members of the Executive Board did not have to be adjusted
due to a malus or clawback in either the reporting period or the previous year. Moreover,
there was no need to temporarily depart from the defined compensation system due to
specific exceptional circumstances.

The compensation of the members of the Executive Board did not have to be adjusted
due to exceeding the maximum compensation set in either the reporting period or the
previous year.

Former Executive Board members who were active during the past ten years received
pension payments of €926,515 in the reporting year (Reiner Winkler €613,727; Dr. Rainer
Martens €312,788).

Compensation of the Supervisory Board
The rules governing Supervisory Board compensation are laid down in the articles of as-
sociation of MTU Aero Engines AG. The compensation is relative to the size of the Group
and the duties and responsibilities of the Supervisory Board members.

Pursuant to Article 12 of the current articles of association of MTU Aero Engines AG,
members of the Supervisory Board receive fixed annual compensation of €80,000,
payable after the end of the fiscal year. The chair of the Supervisory Board receives three
times and the deputy one-and-a-half times the amount of fixed compensation. In addi-
tion to this compensation, members serving on one of the Supervisory Board’s commit-
tees receive an additional €20,000 for the fiscal year and a further €40,000 for the fiscal
year if they chair a committee. Supervisory Board members who are also members of the
Nomination Committee receive an additional €10,000, while the chair of this committee
receives an additional €20,000. Furthermore, members of the Supervisory Board receive
an attendance fee of €3,000 per meeting of the Supervisory Board and its committees,
limited to €3,000 per day. Expenses incurred in connection with the exercise of their
office are reimbursed, as is any value-added tax payable on compensation. The members
of the Supervisory Board do not receive any share-based compensation.

The following table contains an individualized breakdown of the compensation of each
Supervisory Board member in the reporting year (figures exclude value-added tax). The
fixed annual payment and compensation for committee membership are disclosed as
compensation owed and comprise the compensation for the reporting year paid out at
the start of the following year.

                                                                                                       Business activities and markets
The MTU Group                                                                                          «MTU’s portfolio covers the entire lifecycle of commercial and military aircraft engines
                                                                                                       and aero-derivative industrial gas turbines. The company’s activities range from develop-
                                                                                                       ment, manufacturing and sales to maintenance.

                                                                                                       MTU has technological expertise in low-pressure turbines, high-pressure compressors
                                                                                                       and turbine center frames, and in repair techniques and manufacturing processes.
                                                                                                       Through risk- and revenue-sharing partnerships, it is involved in important national and
                                                                                                       international technology programs and cooperates with the top names in the industry
                                                                                                       (GE Aerospace, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce).

                                                                                                       The Group also provides maintenance services for commercial aircraft engines. In the
                                                                                                       military sector, it has been the leading industrial partner to the German armed forces for
                                                                                                       decades.

                                                                                                       MTU operates in two segments: the OEM business (Original Equipment Manufacturing)
                                                                                                       and MRO business (Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul). The OEM segment covers new
                                                                                                       commercial engines, including spare parts, and the whole of the military sector. The MRO
                                                                                                       segment covers the commercial repair and maintenance business. (ESRS 2 SBM-1 40ai,
                                                                                                       40aii)»1

                                                                                                       Group structure, locations and organization
                                                                                                       Through its subsidiaries, joint ventures and equity investments, MTU has a presence in
                                                                                                       all key markets and regions worldwide. Further information on MTU’s shareholdings is
                                                                                                       provided in the Notes to the consolidated financial statements in section I. Accounting poli-
                                                                                                       cies and principles.

               Economic report




                                                                                                  Macroeconomic conditions
Economic report 2025                                                                              At the macro level, economic debate in 2025 was dominated primarily by global trade
                                                                                                  conflicts. In April 2025, the United States announced the introduction of significant tariffs
                                                                                                  against most of its trading partners – a clear break with established trade policy norms.
                                                                                                  The good news is that the adverse impact on the global economy has been relatively
                                                                                                  moderate so far. In its January 2026 World Economic Outlook, the International Monetary
                                                                                                  Fund (IMF) stated that despite increasing protectionism and a shifting global landscape,
                                                                                                  the global economy showed remarkable resilience in 2025. Companies successfully reor-
                                                                                                  ganized their supply chains and front-loaded trade activities in the earlier months of the
                                                                                                  years, leading to a temporary increase in trade flows.

                                                                                                  Global inflation fell to 4.1% in 2025, with industrialized countries stabilizing close to the
                                                                                                  target of 2.5% – slightly below the 2.6% recorded in 2024. Monetary policy has shifted
                                                                                                  from strict tightening to a more moderate approach, leaning toward neutrality or gradu-
                                                                                                  al easing.

                                                                                                  After a strong start to the year, the global economy weakened gradually. Annual global
                                                                                                  GDP growth remained robust at 3.3%, putting it at a similar level to 2024 (source: IMF
                                                                                                  World Economic Outlook, January 2026).

                                                                                                  Of the world’s three largest economic regions, the Eurozone recorded growth of 1.4% in
                                                                                                  2025, a moderate improvement from 0.9% in 2024. Among its members, Germany’s fiscal
                                                                                                  expansion played a key role in sustaining economic activity. This helped the German
                                                                                                  economy to return to positive territory despite modest growth of 0.2%, thus contributing
                                                                                                  to the Eurozone’s overall performance.

                                                                                                  In the United States, growth slowed to 2.1% in 2025 from 2.8% in 2024 as the temporary
                                                                                                  investment boost began to fade, labor markets weakened, and demand became increas-
                                                                                                  ingly impacted by price rises linked to tariffs.

                                                                                                  In China, the country hardest hit by U.S. tariffs, growth was supported by a weaker real
                                                                                                  effective exchange rate and a front-loaded surge in exports to Asian and European part-
                                                                                                  ners at the beginning of the year. Nevertheless, overall development remained subdued

heights. Reported revenue increased by 18.3% to €8,763 million (previous year: €7,411
million). The OEM segment recorded growth of 19.1% before intersegment consolidation.
The MRO segment, which grew by 17.6%, contributed to higher revenue in the reporting
period. Adjusted revenue for the Group amounted to €8,717 million, increasing by 16.4%
compared to the previous year. As the most significant non-recurring factor, revenue-in-
creasing currency-related effects linked to refund liabilities for the GTF™ fleet manage-
ment plan were eliminated in this regard.

In 2025, MTU increased adjusted EBIT in both the OEM and the MRO segment. Adjusted
EBIT was €1,351 million (previous year: €1,050 million). The adjusted EBIT margin was
15.5% (previous year: 14.0%).

MTU continued to grow and invest in 2025. The year under review was shaped by in-
vestments in engine development work for all commercial thrust classes, investments in
the expansion of production capacity at domestic and foreign sites, and investments in
intangible assets in the form of licensing rights for stakes in MRO programs with the aim
of expanding the maintenance and repair business.

In comparison to the previous year, the (adjusted) free cash flow increased to €378
million (previous year: €183 million) as a result of good business development. Burdens
resulted from business-development-related cash outflows for working capital, the
expenses of compensation payments under the GTF™ fleet management plan, cash-
effective capital expenditure for the expansion of the engine leasing business, and the
increase to global production capacities in the OEM and MRO segment. The GTF™ fleet
management plan and the additional investments in the expansion of international pro-
duction capacities will continue to have a significant adverse effect on the (adjusted) free
cash flow in fiscal year 2026.

In MTU’s view, the forecasts published at the beginning of the year and specified in more
detail during the year were essentially met and in some cases exceeded as a result of the
good operating performance in particular.

                                                                                                  Business activities
                                                                                                  MTU AG develops and manufactures components for commercial and military aircraft en-
                                                                                                  gines and aero-derivative industrial gas turbines. The company also carries out mainte-
                                                                                                  nance of military and commercial engines. MTU has technological expertise, in particular,
                                                                                                  in low-pressure turbines, high-pressure compressors and turbine center frames, and in
                                                                                                  repair techniques and manufacturing processes. It is involved in important national and
                                                                                                  international technology programs and cooperates with the top names in the engine
                                                                                                  industry (known as OEMs) – GE Aerospace, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce.

                                                                                                  Macroeconomic conditions
Forecast 2026                                                                                     In its updated outlook from January 2026, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) is
                                                                                                  forecasting a further drop in inflation in 2026. Global consumer price inflation is expect-
                                                                                                  ed to fall to 3.8% in 2026, with a forecast of 2.2% for industrialized countries. Monetary
                                                                                                  policy may take a different trajectory, with central banks adjusting their interest rates
                                                                                                  differently depending on domestic inflation pressure and economic conditions. The IMF
                                                                                                  is estimating that global GDP growth in 2026 will remain stable at 3.3%, identical to 2025
                                                                                                  (Source: IMF World Economic Outlook Update, January 2026).

                                                                                                  GDP growth in the USA is predicted to rise to 2.4%, slightly above the 2025 level, due to
                                                                                                  tax reductions and the easing of interest rates.

                                                                                                  Weak growth of 1.3% is expected for the Eurozone, with increased uncertainty on several
                                                                                                  levels and higher tariffs being the key factors in slowing growth. For Germany, the IMF is
                                                                                                  forecasting improved growth for 2026, but still at a low rate of 1.1%; this growth will be
                                                                                                  bolstered by the recovery of private consumption resulting from higher actual earnings
                                                                                                  and fiscal easing. China’s economy may remain weak over the year ahead with an on-
                                                                                                  going slump in the real estate sector, restrictions on industrial subsidies and the risk of
                                                                                                  a debt/deflation spiral hampering growth and overall productivity. Chinese GDP growth
                                                                                                  might fall to 4.5% in 2026 (Source: IMF World Economic Outlook Update, January 2026).

                                                                                                  The outlook for 2026 is cautiously stable despite some residual risks according to the
                                                                                                  IMF. Political uncertainty, possible disruptions to trade and occasional price peaks for
                                                                                                  commodities could have an adverse effect on growth, while demographic and labor-mar-
                                                                                                  ket-related challenges could obstruct productivity gains in certain economies. Finan-
                                                                                                  cial vulnerabilities and changes in the measurement of technology-related assets also
                                                                                                  require special attention.

                                                                                                  U.S. political developments under President Trump, including tensions in cases like Iran,
                                                                                                  Greenland or Venezuela, indicate an increased risk of abrupt geopolitical and mar-
                                                                                                  ket-based volatility (Source: IMF World Economic Outlook Update, January 2026).

                                                                                                  On the positive side, the OECD believes that breakthroughs in trade negotiations or the
                                                                                                  reduction of trade restrictions could reduce uncertainty and encourage investment. The
                                                                                                  expedited introduction of AI technology combined with structural reforms to promote
                                                                                                  the mobility of labor, labor market participation and digitalization could boost productiv-
                                                                                                  ity and growth over the medium term. Upholding credible fiscal measures and monetary

Future dividend
MTU’s general dividend policy envisages the payment of an attractive dividend. Despite
the persistent effects of the GTF™ fleet management plan, the Company is in a position
to propose a significantly increased dividend for fiscal year 2025.

MTU’s ambition remains unchanged: to achieve a payout ratio of around 40% of the
adjusted net income over the medium term, provided that the cash conversion rate is
sufficient. In view of the payout ratio targeted for 2026, the planned finalization of the
GTF™ fleet management plan and investment in international business growth must be

               Risk and opportunity report




                                                                                                            Risk report
Risk and opportunity report                                                                                 Risks are an inherent part of any entrepreneurial activity. To enable it to take best advan-
                                                                                                            tage of market opportunities and to identify and manage the risks involved, MTU has an
                                                                                                            integrated opportunity and risk management system. This is linked to the Group’s val-
                                                                                                            ue-oriented performance indicators and its organizational structure and ensures lasting
                                                                                                            business success. The system is based on the internationally recognized COSO II Enter-
                                                                                                            prise Risk Management Framework. In order to implement risk management within the
                                                                                                            MTU Group, the central Risk Management department has been established; tasked with
                                                                                                            policy responsibility, this department coordinates reporting via the Risk Officers named
                                                                                                            in company departments and on behalf of senior management. To this end, the central
                                                                                                            department provides binding instructions and supporting materials. These include the
                                                                                                            MTU risk guidelines and extensive checklists, which provide guidance and operational
                                                                                                            support in the risk management process, the aim being to identify risks at an early stage,
                                                                                                            assess their impacts and, where necessary, devise management measures to mitigate
                                                                                                            the risks and/or create opportunities from them.

                                                                                                            Strategy and risk management system

                                                                                                            Control environment
                                                                                                            MTU regards a suitable control environment as being essential for a functioning risk
                                                                                                            management system. The main elements of this are:

                                                                                                            ⁄      management style and philosophy,
                                                                                                            ⁄      integrity and ethical values,
                                                                                                            ⁄      no-blame culture,
                                                                                                            ⁄      staff training and development.

                                                                                                            The MTU Principles require a constructive approach to mistakes, and the company’s lead-
                                                                                                            ership values include a commitment to actively driving change, creating an atmosphere
                                                                                                            of trust, and ensuring continuous improvement. This is supported by lean management
                                                                                                            in all areas of the company, which also aims to create a culture that ensures a function-
                                                                                                            ing risk management system.

Operational risk management takes place at the level of the organizationally separate
units and in the respective subsidiaries. These are responsible for identifying, assessing,
controlling and monitoring the risks in their specific areas, and documenting them in
a centrally available risk management tool. To this end, the organizational units use a
centrally provided risk checklist derived from the risk inventory.

Opportunity category “Financial”
As a large part of the company’s revenue comes from contracts invoiced in U.S. dollars,
especially in the commercial new engines and series business (OEM) and the commercial
spare parts and aftermarket business (OEM, MRO), a strengthening of the U.S. dollar
against the euro would improve MTU’s earnings. If there is a stabilization or short-term
drop in inflation, this would have a positive effect on MTU’s cost structure and hence on
its business results.

See the Risk report for information on how the opportunities identified can be exploited
and the associated risks avoided.

Overall assessment of opportunities
MTU has taken all the organizational measures necessary to recognize potential oppor-
tunities in good time and respond to them adequately. MTU applies the same methods
in its assessment of specific opportunities as it does when evaluating risks. As a con-
servative approach is taken to the identification of opportunities, the opportunities are
necessarily low compared with the risks.

Based on the opportunities identified, MTU anticipates that the earnings opportunities in
2026 are around €33 million (prior year: €10 million), with the OEM segment, especially
the “Programs & Projects” category, accounting for €27 million of this. The liquidity-re-
lated opportunities amount to €45 million (previous year: €73 million), with €27 million
of this attributable to the OEM segment, especially the “Programs & Projects” category.
Opportunities to extend MTU’s range of products and services may initially lead to a
financial burden. In view of the long cycles involved in the business model, these will only
generate positive earnings in subsequent fiscal years. MTU does not currently foresee
any fundamental changes in its opportunities.

Accounting
MTU prepares its consolidated financial statements and interim reports in accordance
with the International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRSs). The Executive Board is
responsible for the financial statements and reports. Financial reporting comprises, in
particular, the consolidated financial statements and the Group management report
(including the Sustainability Statement). In addition, the financial reporting and the audit
include sustainability reporting, together with the audit thereof. The annual financial
statements of MTU Aero Engines AG are compiled in accordance with the provisions of
the German Commercial Code (HGB). An internal control system, coupled with the appli-
cation of uniform accounting policies, should ensure that the results of operations, finan-
cial position, net assets and cash flows of all Group companies are accurately presented.
In addition, MTU has a differentiated system in place to identify and monitor business
and financial risks.

Risk management and control system
The aim of the Executive Board is to ensure that the company has an appropriate and
effective risk management and control system. To this end, the Group’s risk and oppor-
tunity situation and how it is determined are evaluated at an Executive Board meeting
at least once a quarter; moreover, every six months, the status of the internal control
system is discussed and an overall assessment of its appropriateness and effectiveness
is made. Based on this, the Executive Board has not found any indication that either the
overall entire risk management system or the overall internal control system might not
be appropriate or effective.1 MTU takes findings and suggestions for optimization result-
ing from audits by the Internal Group Audit function and external audits as an oppor-
tunity to make continuous improvements to the risk management system and internal
control system. The systems are described in the section headed Internal control and risk
management system.

               Group Sustainability Statement




The company has identified several stakeholder groups and utilizes various forms of
engagement with each group. In general, MTU’s key stakeholders can be clustered
into two groups: affected stakeholders and users of the sustainability statement.
Affected stakeholders are individuals or groups whose interests are affected or could
be affected—positively or negatively—by MTU’s activities and its direct and indirect
business relationships across its value chain. Affected stakeholders include, for example,
workers in the upstream value chain and nature as a silent stakeholder. Users of MTU’s
sustainability statements are primary users of general financial reporting (existing
and potential investors, lenders, capital markets, associations and organizations,
policymakers and authorities, scientists and researchers, as well as the media). In
addition, a large number of affected stakeholders are also users of the sustainability
statement, such as business partners and customers, analysts and rating agencies,
trade unions and social partners, employees, suppliers, and regional stakeholders. The
following table contains an overview of MTU’s most important stakeholders, the type
of stakeholder engagement, the stakeholder interests recorded, and actions taken in
response to their interests.

As a result of the double materiality assessment, the positive impacts of MTU’s MRO
activities on resource use and circular economy, specifically the subtopic of resource
outflows, were assessed as material. For example, the product design creates the basis
for the application of various circular economy strategies, such as repairability (MTU OEM
sites). The various circular economy strategies (refuse, reuse, repair) are implemented
directly through maintenance activities (MTU MRO sites). In this context, high-pressure
compressors, low-pressure turbines, and turbine center frames for the commercial
or military aviation sector as well as for industrial gas turbines are considered to be
significant resource outflows. To manufacture these products, MTU mainly uses super
alloys and titanium alloys. The MRO activities result in an increased service life of the
products, among other things, thereby helping to conserve resources.

MTU did not hold any consultations as part of the materiality assessment.

With regard to the classification of an economic activity as “environmentally sustainable”
within the meaning of the EU Taxonomy, a distinction has to be drawn between those
activities that are taxonomy-eligible and those that are taxonomy-aligned. Only those
economic activities that can be assigned to the descriptions of the activities in the
delegated acts, irrespective of whether the technical screening criteria are met, are
deemed to be taxonomy-eligible.

                                                                                                           Climate change mitigation in MTU’s own business operations
                                                                                                           With its ecoRoadmap, MTU aims to permanently reduce the use of fossil fuels and
                                                                                                           greenhouse gas emissions at its own production and maintenance sites. The previous
                                                                                                           target of reducing Scope 1 and market-based Scope 2 emissions by 60% by 2030
                                                                                                           compared to the base year 2019 had already led to a 42.2% reduction in emissions by
                                                                                                           2024. The target was updated in the 2025 reporting year: By 2035, Scope 1 and market-
                                                                                                           based Scope 2 emissions are to be reduced by 63% compared to the new base year of
                                                                                                           2024, and reduced by 90% by 2050. Unavoidable remaining emissions are to be offset
                                                                                                           by permanent CO₂ removal and storage solutions. The new base year 2024 was chosen
                                                                                                           to cover the integration of the MTU maintenance site in Fort Worth, which has been fully
                                                                                                           consolidated since the end of 2024, into the target architecture. When setting its Scope 1
                                                                                                           and 2 targets, MTU was guided by the European Green Deal and the underlying objective
                                                                                                           of the Paris Agreement, which aims to limit global warming to 1.5°C.

Procedural instructions for evaluation of environmental aspects in product design
Content                     These procedural instructions describe how environmentally relevant aspects are considered in
                            product design. During the product design phase, environmentally relevant aspects (such as low
                            consumption and reduced emissions in the production and use phases) are evaluated by the
                            designer and consulting departments. MTU’s design system should ensure that this evaluation is
                            possible and is checked at defined points in the development process. The system guidelines
                            describe, among other things, which environmentally relevant aspects are directly determined or
                            indirectly influenced by product design.
                            This policy addresses climate change mitigation and energy efficiency related to MTU’s products.

Target                      Reduction of environmental impacts both in the use phase as well as in manufacturing and
                            maintenance (such as low consumption and reduced emissions). Additionally, the use of more
                            environmentally friendly materials and operating substances as well as the selection of materials
                            with high recyclability.

Associated material         MTU’s products are modules for engines in the aviation sector. The emissions generated by these
impacts, risks and          products during the use phase have an actual negative impact on the environment by
opportunities               contributing to global warming.

Monitoring                  To ensure that environmentally relevant aspects are taken into account in product design, the
                            MTU planning system defines points in product development at which the current state of
                            development is checked (e.g. technical reviews and gate reviews). As part of this process,
                            questionnaires containing documentation of the design evaluation based on environmentally
                            relevant criteria must be completed.

Scope                       The policies are decisive in the development of new products and affect all technical departments
                            involved in development at the following sites:
                            ⁄   MTU Aero Engines AG (Munich)
                            ⁄   MTU Aero Engines North America Inc.
                            ⁄   MTU Aero Engines Polska sp. z o.o.

Responsible                 The Engineering Office is responsible for implementing and monitoring the procedural
organizational level        instructions for evaluation of environmental aspects in product design.

Availability                The policy is not publicly available and can be accessed only via the document management
                            system for MTU employees.

Climate Transition Plan guidelines
Content                                              The guidelines, including associated annexes, set out the policies for MTU’s transition to a low-emission and climate-resilient company.
                                                     They cover the initial situation of climate management, strategic ambitions, reduction paths, accounting, target setting, risk assessment, and approaches to implementing and financing actions.

Target                                               The guidelines aim to address the risks of climate change for MTU and at the same time promote the integration of sustainability matters into the company’s business strategy and business model. They
                                                     emphasize the need to act to reduce emissions and adapt operations, not only to protect the company from potential risks, but also to seize opportunities to innovate and meet growing stakeholder
                                                     demands for sustainable business practices.

Associated material impacts, risks and               In the development, manufacture, and maintenance of aircraft engines, MTU generates emissions that have negative impacts on the climate. One risk for MTU is that corporate growth and high locked-in
opportunities                                        emissions could jeopardize the achievement of climate change mitigation targets, while at the same time new regulations could lead to higher ticket prices and increase the attractiveness of alternative
                                                     mobility solutions. This in turn would reduce demand for flights and lead to a loss of revenue in OEM sales and maintenance services.

Monitoring                                           The Climate Transition Board supports the implementation and progress of climate change mitigation actions on the basis of defined metrics with clearly assigned responsibilities. An interdisciplinary team
                                                     of experts works across departments to further develop and apply methods for evaluating and optimizing climate change mitigation actions and secures their integration into the relevant specialist
                                                     functions. This structure aims to ensure that all key aspects of the climate transition are implemented in a coordinated, consistent manner and with the involvement of all divisions concerned. Regular
                                                     progress reports are submitted to the Corporate Sustainability Board and the Executive Board.

Scope                                                All MTU locations under operational control:
                                                     ⁄   MTU Aero Engines AG (Munich)
                                                     ⁄   MTU Aero Engines North America Inc.
                                                     ⁄   MTU Aero Engines Polska sp. z o.o.
                                                     ⁄   MTU Aero Engines (Shanghai) Ltd.
                                                     ⁄   MTU Maintenance Australia Pty. Ltd.
                                                     ⁄   MTU Maintenance Berlin-Brandenburg GmbH
                                                     ⁄   MTU Maintenance Canada Ltd.
                                                     ⁄   MTU Maintenance do Brasil Ltda.
                                                     ⁄   MTU Maintenance Fort Worth Inc.
                                                     ⁄   MTU Maintenance Hannover GmbH
                                                     ⁄   MTU Maintenance Lease Services B.V.
                                                     ⁄   MTU Maintenance Serbia d.o.o.
                                                     ⁄   MTU Maintenance Service Center Ayutthaya Ltd.
                                                     ⁄   MTU Maintenance Singapore Pte. Ltd.
                                                     ⁄   3D.aero GmbH
                                                     ⁄   eMoSys GmbH


                                                     They account for 100% of MTU’s Scope 1 and location-based Scope 2 emissions in 2025.

Responsible organizational level                     The bodies responsible for implementing the climate protection manual are the departments of climate and environmental protection, purchasing & logistics, finance, and development & technology as
                                                     well as, at the management level, the Executive Board and CSO.

MTUPlus Intelligent Solutions: PERFORMPlus (smart repairs) and ValuePlus (smart reuse)
Key actions taken and outcomes achieved             Smart repairs
                                                    MTU’s MRO services are tailored to the customer’s specific requirements. Whenever possible, repairs are carried out on the wing or at the customer’s premises. This reduces downtimes as well as total
                                                    costs, and extends the on-wing times of the engines. MTU Engine Fleet Management and Engine Trend Monitoring enable intelligent fleet management and proactive maintenance planning.
                                                    Determining optimum maintenance cycles is done based on measurement points such as exhaust gas temperatures, fuel consumption, and thrust combined with historical wear data and customer
                                                    feedback. Furthermore, various factors such as a potential drop in performance on the wing, component wear, and the (remaining) useful life are taken into account. The scope of maintenance actions
                                                    is also planned on the basis of these metrics and, if necessary, adjusted based on further findings during disassembly and inspection. Continuous development of innovative measurement methods
                                                    enables more efficient damage detection, increased damage repair, and thus an extension of the service life of the components.
                                                    Smart reuse
                                                    With regard to maintenance strategies for mature engines, it can be more beneficial to prioritize the installation of used spare parts instead of new parts. For this purpose, MTU identifies suitable used/
                                                    decommissioned engines, disassembles them, reconditions the reusable components, and installs them in in-service engines. In addition, the company also sells used and reconditioned spare parts.

MTUPlus Intelligent Solutions: PERFORMPlus (smart repairs) and ValuePlus (smart reuse)
Key actions planned and time horizons for            MTU aims to successively improve and expand the aforementioned circular economy strategies (especially reuse and repair). The following actions are planned for the period until 2030:
implementation                                       ⁄   Develop a metrics system for evaluating circular economy activities with a special focus on maintenance
                                                         As part of a collaboration with the Institute of Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul at the German Aerospace Center, the ecological impact of MTU maintenance actions is systematically evaluated with
                                                         the help of a lifecycle assessment. The company also plans to develop further indicators that take into account the criticality of raw materials and other aspects of the circular economy. In the future,
                                                         a comprehensive metrics system will be available that will enable the holistic optimization of maintenance cycles and actions.
                                                     ⁄   Expand inspection and repair capabilities
                                                         MTU is continuously working on expanding its inspection and repair capabilities. One example here is the development of a borescope solution that enables improved inspection of engines directly
                                                         on-site, thus avoiding costly transportation to MRO sites. The company also plans to expand its repair capabilities in order to meet the rising demand for component repairs and to be able to offer
                                                         suitable repair processes more quickly once the program has been launched. One part of this plan involved setting up an international repair network at the organizational level, which will allow
                                                         more homogeneous capacity utilization and the targeted use of site-specific skills in the future. It also entails driving forward the industrialization of various repair processes, such as special coating
                                                         or joining processes. This increases the service life of the parts and avoids the use of primary materials for the manufacture of new parts.
                                                     ⁄   Predict engine condition down to the parts level for application-optimized maintenance
                                                         MTU aims to develop a prediction model that makes it possible to quantify the engine wear down to the parts level on the basis of the intended flight routes and ambient conditions. The findings
                                                         will enable the further optimization of maintenance cycles. Furthermore, a better understanding of wear and tear in relation to ambient conditions can increase the service life of parts, enable
                                                         more targeted development of repair processes, and promote the reuse of used parts. The planned prediction model will also enable a quantity-based estimation of material flows that are sent for
                                                         recycling. This has the potential to promote monomaterial recycling, as this is usually only economical for certain quantities of material.
                                                     ⁄   Systematically screen air fleets for future spare parts
                                                         MTU is currently working to develop a system that will enable more efficient identification of suitable spare parts. This system is intended to provide a more precise assessment of the condition of
                                                         parts at the component level for engines in operation. The assessment will be based on application and use data.
                                                     MTU also plans to be developing and using digital twins of engines (virtual versions) across all life cycles by 2035. This is intended to accelerate the development of new products by minimizing design
                                                     iterations, improve the recyclability of products, and enable the early development of suitable repair processes. The latter can help in particular to conserve resources, as damaged parts often have to
                                                     be replaced with new parts in the first two years after the start of the program due to a lack of repair procedures.

Contribution to the policy objectives and            One objective of the procedural instructions for evaluation of environmental aspects in product design is the development of resource-efficient repair processes in the MRO segment. The implementa-
requirements                                         tion of the above actions leads to significantly shorter maintenance times, for example by adapting the scope of repairs to usage and thus to lower energy and material consumption. On-wing
                                                     inspections reduce transportation costs. The consumption of resources is reduced by using spare parts from decommissioned engines and by optimizing the product design, for example to reduce
                                                     component wear. In summary, all the above actions help to ensure compliance with the requirements of the procedural instructions.

Scope                                                Unless explicitly stated otherwise, the actions apply to all MRO sites.

Progress                                             The aforementioned actions with regard to the smart repair and reuse of used parts are continuously implemented, optimized, and expanded. Progress was made in, among other areas, digitalization,
                                                     which enables more efficient detection and analysis of damage in the MRO business. In addition, initial findings on the environmental impact of maintenance actions have already been obtained.

MTU recognizes the respect and protection of human rights as fundamental values
and opposes exploitative working conditions in any form. In particular, MTU strongly
condemns child labor in all its forms. MTU is convinced that children need access to
education in order to be able to develop without the risk of entering the workforce too
early. The dignity of children must be respected, and their safety and health must be
protected. Should MTU employ minors, for example in the context of apprenticeships,
it strictly adheres to the core labor standards of the International Labour Organization
(ILO), particularly concerning minimum age requirements. Employment relationships at
MTU are voluntary and can be terminated by employees at any time of their own free

strategy.
